concepts.name: Sources for Chandragupta Maurya's History: Literary vs. Archaeological
key_dimensions: Greek/Classical sources (Megasthenes' Indica, Justin, Plutarch) vs. Indian sources (Arthashastra, Mudrarakshasa, Puranas) — their biases and limitations
Archaeological corroboration: Ashokan edicts as indirect evidence, Sanchi, Pataliputra excavations
UPSC trap: Megasthenes never mentions Chandragupta by name ('Sandrokottos' identification controversy and its resolution by William Jones)
Jain sources (Parisishtaparvan by Hemachandra) vs. Buddhist sources (Mahavamsa, Dipavamsa) — differing narratives on his origins

concepts.name: Chandragupta's Origins and Early Life: The Historiographical Debate
key_dimensions: Brahmanical/Puranic tradition: lowly/Shudra origin vs. Buddhist tradition: Kshatriya/Moriya clan of Pippalivana
Jain tradition: connection to peacock tamers (Mayura-poshaka) — etymology of 'Maurya'
Greek accounts: Justin's reference to humble birth ('humili quidem genere ortus')
UPSC trap: No single accepted theory — examiners may test which source says what, not which is 'correct'

concepts.name: Role of Chanakya (Kautilya/Vishnugupta) in Chandragupta's Rise
key_dimensions: Chanakya's three identities: Kautilya (author of Arthashastra), Vishnugupta (personal name), Chanakya (patronymic from father Chanaka)
Political-strategic mentorship: training at Taxila, strategic planning for Nanda overthrow
Mudrarakshasa (Vishakhadatta) narrative: dramatic account of Chanakya's role — its value as historical source vs. literary fiction
UPSC trap: Arthashastra authorship debate — R. Shamasastry's 1909 discovery; debate on whether it is solely Kautilya's work or a compiled text

concepts.name: Overthrow of the Nanda Dynasty: Strategies and Significance
key_dimensions: Nanda Empire's strengths (vast army per Greek accounts) vs. internal weaknesses (unpopular rule, brahmin resentment under Dhana Nanda)
Chandragupta's military strategy: guerrilla warfare in early phase, alliance-building with frontier chieftains
Chanakya's political strategy: use of spies, subversion of Nanda ministers (especially Rakshasa)
UPSC trap: The 'first attempt' failure narrative in Mudrarakshasa — strategic lesson of not attacking the center first (peripheral strategy)

concepts.name: Alexander's Invasion and Its Impact on Chandragupta's Rise
key_dimensions: Power vacuum in northwest India after Alexander's death (323 BCE) and withdrawal of Macedonian garrisons
Possible meeting between young Chandragupta and Alexander — Plutarch's account (Alexander 'offended' by Androcottus) and its reliability
How Alexander's invasion fragmented northwest, enabling Chandragupta to fill the void
UPSC trap: Alexander never reached Magadha — his army mutinied at Beas (Hyphasis); conflating his 'conquest of India' with actual Magadha is a common error

concepts.name: Conquest of Northwestern India and Defeat of Seleucus Nicator
key_dimensions: Chandragupta's recapture of northwestern territories (Punjab, Sindh) from Macedonian satraps post-Alexander
War with Seleucus I Nicator (305–303 BCE): outcome — Treaty of the Indus
Terms of the Treaty: Seleucus ceded territories (Arachosia, Gedrosia, Paropamisadae, Aria) in exchange for 500 war elephants
UPSC trap: This is the ONLY instance of a Mauryan ruler defeating a Hellenistic successor king; the elephant diplomacy had decisive impact at Battle of Ipsus (301 BCE)

concepts.name: The Treaty of the Indus (303 BCE): Territorial and Diplomatic Dimensions
key_dimensions: Territories ceded by Seleucus: modern Afghanistan and Balochistan regions — extent of Mauryan Empire's northwest
Marriage alliance clause: Seleucus gave his daughter (or a princess) to Chandragupta — 'Epigamia' (intermarriage rights between Greeks and Indians)
Appointment of Megasthenes as ambassador to Pataliputra — source of Indica
UPSC trap: Epigamia is often misread as solely a dynastic marriage; it legally permitted intermarriage between the two peoples — a broader diplomatic concept

concepts.name: Conquest of Magadha and Establishment of Mauryan Capital at Pataliputra
key_dimensions: Pataliputra (modern Patna) as administrative capital — its strategic location at confluence of Ganga, Son, and Punpun rivers
Megasthenes' description of Pataliputra: size, wooden palisade, 570 towers, 64 gates — archaeological corroboration (wooden remains at Kumrahar)
Transition from Nanda capital to Mauryan capital — continuity vs. change in administration
UPSC trap: Pataliputra was founded by Ajatashatru (Udayin), not by Chandragupta — he inherited and expanded it

concepts.name: Extent of Chandragupta's Empire: Geographic Boundaries
key_dimensions: Northern frontier: Hindu Kush/Hindukush after Seleucid treaty; Eastern: Bengal/Magadha heartland; Western: Saurashtra (Girnar inscription of Rudradaman mentions Mauryan governor Pushyagupta)
Southern expansion: extent debated — whether Chandragupta himself reached Deccan or this was Bindusara's achievement
UPSC trap: Kalinga was NOT part of Chandragupta's empire — it was conquered by Ashoka; confusing the three Mauryan emperors' conquests is a classic trap
Comparison with later Mauryan extent under Ashoka — what Chandragupta established vs. what was added later

concepts.name: Mauryan Administrative System Under Chandragupta: Arthashastra as Blueprint
key_dimensions: Central administration: King → Mantriparishad (council of ministers) → departmental heads (Adhyakshas) — 18 Tirthas listed in Arthashastra
Provincial administration: four provinces under Kumara (princes) with Mahamatyas; Girnar (West), Tosali (East), Suvarnagiri (South), Taxila (North)
Espionage system (Gudhapurusha): Chanakya's elaborate spy network — classification of spies in Arthashastra
UPSC trap: The Arthashastra describes an ideal/prescriptive state; conflating it entirely with actual Mauryan practice is methodologically flawed

concepts.name: Mauryan Military Organization Under Chandragupta
key_dimensions: Megasthenes' account: six-board military committee of 30 members divided into five sub-committees (navy, infantry, cavalry, war chariots, elephants, commissariat)
Size of Chandragupta's army: Pliny's figure of 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry, 9,000 elephants — reliability and exaggeration debate
Role of war elephants as a strategic asset — their decisive role in Seleucid treaty and Battle of Ipsus
UPSC trap: The six-board system described by Megasthenes — examinees often miscount the committees or confuse with Arthashastra's military organization

concepts.name: Economic and Revenue Administration: Arthashastra Principles
key_dimensions: Land revenue as primary source: Bhaga (1/6th share), various taxes listed in Arthashastra
State monopolies: salt, mining, forests, arms manufacture — 'Sita' lands (crown lands) vs. privately cultivated lands
Punch-marked coins (Karshapana) as evidence of monetized economy under Mauryas
UPSC trap: The Arthashastra mentions 'Saptanga' (seven elements of state) — often confused with Ashoka's Dhamma concept; these are entirely different frameworks

concepts.name: Chandragupta's Conversion to Jainism and Abdication
key_dimensions: Jain tradition: Chandragupta became a disciple of Jain monk Bhadrabahu and migrated to Shravanabelagola (Karnataka)
Practice of Sallekhana (ritual fasting unto death) at Shravanabelagola — Jain tradition vs. historical skepticism
Political implication of abdication: transfer of power to son Bindusara — stability of succession

UPSC trap: Shravanabelagola is primarily associated with the Bahubali (Gomateshwara) statue (10th century CE Ganga dynasty), NOT with Chandragupta directly — the cave associated with him is a separate, smaller site

concepts.name: Chanakya's Arthashastra: Content, Dating, and Historical Significance
key_dimensions: Structure: 15 Books (Adhikaranas), 150 chapters covering statecraft, economics, military strategy, law, diplomacy
Mandala theory (Circle of States): friend's enemy is a friend; elaboration of six-fold policy (Shadgunya)
Dating controversy: composed by Kautilya (4th century BCE) vs. later redaction (3rd century CE) — R.P. Kangle vs. Patrick Olivelle debate
UPSC trap: Arthashastra was 'lost' and rediscovered in 1905 by R. Shamasastry (not 1909 — the publication was 1909, discovery/manuscript receipt was 1904–05); examinees often get the date wrong

concepts.name: Megasthenes' Indica: Value and Limitations as a Historical Source
key_dimensions: Original text lost — survives only in fragments quoted by later writers (Diodorus, Strabo, Arrian, Pliny)
Accurate observations: Pataliputra's description, seven castes of Indians (his classification differs from varna), fertile agriculture, absence of slavery (contradicted by Indian sources)
Inaccuracies/Exaggerations: denial of famine in India, fantastical creatures, misunderstanding of Indian social structure
UPSC trap: Megasthenes says Indians had NO slavery — but Arthashastra and other sources mention 'Dasa' (slaves); this contradiction is a high-yield analytical question

concepts.name: The Saptanga Theory (Seven Elements of State) in Arthashastra
key_dimensions: Seven elements: Swami (king), Amatya (ministers), Janapada (territory/people), Durga (fort), Kosha (treasury), Danda (army), Mitra (ally)
Comparative analysis with modern state elements — sovereignty, territory, government, population
Hierarchy and interdependence of the seven elements — king as the most important but dependent on others
UPSC trap: Often confused with the Ashta-pradhan of Marathas or with Mauryan administrative tiers — the Saptanga is a theoretical/philosophical construct, not an organizational chart

concepts.name: Synchronism of Chandragupta with Greek Records: The Cornerstone of Indian Chronology
key_dimensions: William Jones' 1793 identification of 'Sandrokottos' of Greek records with Chandragupta Maurya — foundation of Indian historical chronology
How this synchronism anchors Indian chronology: Alexander's death (323 BCE) → Chandragupta's accession (~321 BCE) becomes a fixed point
Revisionist challenge: Oak, Feuerstein etc. rejecting this synchronism — mainstream rejection of such revisionism and why
UPSC trap: This synchronism is called the 'sheet-anchor' of Indian chronology — the specific term and its significance; also note it was Jones, not later scholars, who established it

concepts.name: Chandragupta's Conquests in the Deccan: Evidence and Debate
key_dimensions: Girnar (Junagadh) Rock Inscription of Rudradaman (150 CE): mentions Mauryan governor Pushyagupta built Sudarshana Lake — indirect evidence of Mauryan presence in Saurashtra under Chandragupta
Jain tradition of Chandragupta's southern journey to Shravanabelagola implies southern campaigns
Debate: Was the Deccan conquered by Chandragupta or Bindusara? — most historians attribute some southern expansion to Chandragupta, full Deccan to Bindusara

UPSC trap: The Sudarshana Lake inscription is one of the OLDEST datable non-Ashokan references to a Mauryan emperor — its multi-layered history (Pushyagupta → Tushaspa under Ashoka → Rudradaman repairs) is frequently tested

concepts.name: Chandragupta's Legacy: Foundational Significance of the Mauryan State
key_dimensions: First pan-Indian empire: political unification of Indian subcontinent for the first time — significance for Indian national identity narrative
Institutional legacy: centralized bureaucracy, standardized coinage, organized military — continuity into Ashokan period
Diplomatic precedent: first documented exchange of ambassadors between Indian and Western states (Megasthenes)
UPSC trap: Chandragupta is often romanticized as unifier of 'all India' — but northeastern India (parts), far south, and Kalinga remained outside his empire; precision on extent is critical
